The problem asks for the smallest number of initially infected sections, $k$, in a $64 \times 64$ petri dish such that any initial configuration of $k$ infected sections will always lead to a full infection. The rules are: 1) A $2 \times 2$ square with three infected sections becomes completely infected. 2) A $2 \times 2$ square with exactly two infected sections flips all four sections (infected become sterile, and vice-versa). 

Let $n=64$. We examine the parities of the rows $r_i$ and columns $c_j$. Rule 2 preserves all $r_i$ and $c_j$ because flipping all four cells in a $2 \times 2$ block changes the sum of each row and column in that block by 2, which is $0 \pmod 2$. Rule 1 flips exactly one $r_i$ and one $c_j$. 

The parity of $N_r = \sum r_i$ and $N_c = \sum c_j$ must satisfy $N_r \equiv N_c \pmod 2$ because both are equal to the total number of infected sections modulo 2. Rule 1 changes $N_r$ and $N_c$ by $\pm 1$, so $N_r - N_c \pmod 2$ remains 0. However, as established earlier, $N_r = N_c$ always holds. 

In the final state of all infected sections, $r_i = n \pmod 2$ and $c_j = n \pmod 2$. For $n=64$, $r_i = 0$ and $c_j
